people.desc: Rhoda Weaver works nights as an ER nurse at Lancaster General. She was raised in a conservative Mennonite family near New Holland and now belongs to a Lancaster Mennonite Conference congregation that stopped wearing the covering when she was a teenager. She spent two years with Mennonite Central Committee in Haiti in her twenties, keeps bees, and has three teenagers and a husband who repairs farm machinery. She is blunt, dry and quick to laugh, and has little patience for church people who talk more than they help; a cousin who left an Amish family and was shunned still skips the reunions, and Rhoda has never made peace with that.

notes.note: She thinks wealth makes it very hard to use it well. 'Nothing wrong' is more than she would say, but she would not say something is wrong with her brother's dairy either. Not sure is near enough.
She would lie to an abuser looking for his wife in the ER. But she grew up on 'let your yes be yes' and tapped Agree with a wince.
She would follow God over family, but she would want the congregation to test the call first. A private sense of calling is not enough for her.
A church should hold its members accountable. 'Put out' reads to her as shunning, which she watched hurt her cousin, so she went with Disagree.
Following Jesus takes daily work, but 'up to you' leaves out grace and the church that holds you up. Disagree, loosely.

people.overall: Plain and quick, and she liked that it never asked her to sign off on doctrine words. The ones on lying, war and putting members out touched things her own church still argues about, and she wanted a line to explain herself.

people.seed: Irish Catholic widower whose wife died last year, 66, Boston
people.desc: Frank Donnelly is a retired pipefitter from Dorchester who now lives in Quincy. His wife Maureen died of pancreatic cancer fourteen months ago, after forty-one years of marriage. He has gone to the 7 a.m. Mass most days since, partly for God and partly because the house is too quiet, though he is still furious with the archdiocese over the abuse cover-up and says so to anyone. He jokes his way out of feelings, claims to hate the parish grief group his daughter signed him up for and has never missed it, and twice he has dreamed Maureen was in the kitchen telling him to eat something green.

notes.note: He dreamed of Maureen and it felt like more than a dream. Whether that was God or her, he could not say. Agree was the nearest.
He wants the priests who abused children and the bishops who hid them put out, but not his divorced daughter. No single answer covers both, so he tapped Not sure.
He means you have to do your part. He knows the priest would say grace comes first, but that is not how it feels at 66.
He hopes so, for Maureen's brother who never went to church. The nuns taught him otherwise, and 'will' is surer than he can be.

people.overall: The one about weeping stopped him, and he sat with it a while before tapping. The rest was plain enough that it did not feel like a catechism test, which he was braced for.

people.seed: Stand-up comedian, lapsed Catholic, 34, New York
people.desc: Tess Villanueva is a Filipino-American comic from Woodside, Queens, with twelve years of Catholic school behind her. She quit law school at 25 to do stand-up while her parents cried about it. She only goes to Mass for midnight Mass with her mother at Christmas, but she mutters a Hail Mary on the 7 train before every set that matters and does ten minutes on her lola's rosary. She is quick, anxious, very online, in therapy, and recovered from an eating disorder in her twenties; she thinks she probably believes in God and definitely does not believe in bishops.

notes.note: First thought: 'I talk for a living.' She would agree a joke is better with fewer words, but she answered for life, not for sets.
'Closer to God' assumes she is close at all. She answered for the subway Hail Marys, which do feel more real to her than Mass.
Rich is fine; billionaires are not. The 'as long as' part felt like it was doing a lot of work, and she disagreed with the spirit of it.
It hit a nerve. She agreed with what she is working toward in recovery, not with how she feels about her body most days.
She read it as her own story, leaving law school for comedy against her parents. Whether that was God calling, she has no idea.

people.overall: Faster and less preachy than she expected, and nothing asked her to say she believed anything. She caught herself answering a few items for her own non-religious version of them, like a calling or praying alone, and wondered if that counts.

people.desc: Jenna Hollis lives outside Boise with her engineer husband and five children, whom she homeschools with a classical curriculum heavy on Latin, Plato and Augustine. She was raised without religion in Portland, became a Christian through a campus ministry in college, and now teaches the women's study on the Westminster Confession at her PCA church. She loves a good argument, laughs easily, and paints watercolour landscapes on Saturday mornings. She is uneasy with the loud Christian-nationalist crowd in some Idaho churches, which surprises people who assume she is one of them.

notes.note: Augustine says never lie; Rahab and the Hebrew midwives complicate it. She wanted to separate lying from deceiving someone who has no right to the truth, so Not sure.
'Books' is vague. If it means the Bible, strongly disagree; nature shows God's power but not the gospel. She paints landscapes, so she did not go all the way.
The body is good and will be raised, but the flesh has to be put to death. The sentence blurs body and flesh.
Both matter, and the deeper meaning depends on it having happened. The sentence makes her pick one, so Disagree.
She is wary of a private feeling of 'calling'. If Scripture plainly requires it, yes. She thought of her own parents when she was baptised.
Only for serious, unrepentant sin after due process, and by Scripture's standards rather than 'its standards'.
She wants laws that honour God's law but not a state church, and dislikes the Christian-nationalist crowd. 'Support the faith' could mean either, so Not sure.

people.overall: Quick and enjoyable, but she kept wanting to add a clause; several statements felt like two claims she would answer differently. She recognised the calm-heart one as the Stoics and liked that the quiz did not tip its hand.

people.seed: Anglican university student, 22, Nairobi, son of a bishop
people.desc: Daniel Mwangi studies economics at the University of Nairobi and is the eldest son of an Anglican Church of Kenya bishop. The family assumes he will be ordained; he wants to work at the Central Bank. He leads worship on guitar at the youth service, marched in the 2024 protests against the Finance Bill, and is angry that churches take cash from politicians at fundraisers. His grandmother came to faith in the East African Revival and still tells how she dreamed of his birth before it happened; he is warm and respectful in public and argues hard with his father at home.

notes.note: He despises the prosperity preachers and corrupt MPs but wants to do well himself. 'Use it well' is what let him agree.
In his family the pressure runs the other way: they beg him to be ordained. Honouring his father weighs heavily, and the sentence does not fit his case, so Not sure.
He wants Christian values in Kenyan law, but he is sick of politicians buying pulpits with cash. 'Support' could mean either; he went with his anger.
Hustle culture says yes; his father's sermons say grace. He left it at Not sure.

people.overall: Easy to read and fast. A few statements pulled between what his father preaches and what he actually thinks, which he found more interesting than he expected; the one about governments sounded a little American to him.
